goals: Describe the roles of the cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary muscles and retina
Explain the power of accommodation, the near point and the far point
Explain myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia with ray diagrams

slides.heading: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how the eye forms an image, how it **adjusts its focus**, and how spectacles correct common **defects of vision**.
slides.narration: Namaste! Right now your eyes are reading these words, judging colours and adjusting for the light in your room, all without you noticing. The eye is a living camera with a lens that changes its own shape. In this part we see how it works, why some people need spectacles, and how an optician decides the power of those spectacles.

slides.heading: Parts of the human eye
slides.body_md: The eyeball is nearly spherical, about **2.3 cm** across. Light passes through the **cornea**, the **pupil** and the **eye lens** to the **retina**.

visual.caption: The iris is coloured (here brown); the pupil is the hole in its centre.

slides.narration: Trace the path of light on the diagram. It first meets the cornea, the clear curved window at the front. Then it crosses a watery liquid, passes through the pupil in the coloured iris, goes through the eye lens and the jelly-like vitreous humour, and lands on the retina at the back. The optic nerve carries the message from the retina to the brain.

slides.heading: What each part does

rows: Transparent front bulge; **most of the refraction** of light happens at its outer surface
Dark muscular diaphragm that **controls the size of the pupil**
Opening that **regulates the amount of light** entering the eye
Fine adjustment of focal length; forms a **real, inverted** image on the retina
Change the **curvature** (and so the focal length) of the eye lens
Light-sensitive layer; its cells send **electrical signals** through the optic nerve to the brain

visual.alt: Table of eye parts and their roles: cornea refracts most of the light, iris controls pupil size, pupil regulates light, lens adjusts focus and forms a real inverted image, ciliary muscles change lens curvature, retina converts light into electrical signals

slides.narration: Each part has one main job. Here is a surprise for many students: the cornea, not the lens, does most of the bending of light. The lens only fine-tunes the focus. The retina is covered with light-sensitive cells that turn light into electrical signals, and the brain turns those signals into the picture you see, the right way up.

slides.heading: From light to sight
slides.body_md: The image on the retina is **real and inverted**. The brain processes the signals so that we see objects as they are.

visual.alt: Flow chart: light from an object passes through the cornea, pupil and eye lens to form a real inverted image on the retina; electrical signals travel along the optic nerve to the brain, which gives an upright picture

slides.narration: Think of it as a relay race. Light is bent by the cornea and the lens and forms a small, upside-down image on the retina. The retina changes the light into electrical signals. The optic nerve carries them to the brain, which interprets them so that the world looks upright. Seeing really happens in the brain.

slides.heading: Quick check: controlling the light
slides.body_md: Which part of the eye controls the size of the pupil?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that the pupil is just an opening. Ask yourself which part has the muscles that make that opening bigger or smaller.

slides.heading: The pupil in bright and dim light
slides.body_md: In **bright light** the iris makes the pupil **small**; in **dim light** it opens the pupil **wide**. This takes a little time.

rows: Lets in less light, protecting the retina
Lets in more light so dim objects can be seen
Walking into the dark hall from sunlight
For a short time you cannot see the seats clearly

visual.alt: Table: in bright light the pupil contracts to let in less light; in a dark hall it expands to let in more; walking from sunlight into a dark hall you see poorly until the pupil has expanded

slides.narration: Walk from a sunny street into a dark cinema hall and for a few moments you can hardly see the seats. Your pupils were small in the bright sunlight. The iris now has to open them wide to let in more light, and that takes a little time. Coming out again, the bright light feels harsh until the pupils shrink.

slides.heading: Power of accommodation
slides.body_md: The ability of the eye lens to **change its focal length** so that both near and distant objects are seen clearly is the **power of accommodation**.

slides.narration: The distance from lens to retina is fixed, so the eye focuses by changing the lens itself. For a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin and its focal length increases. For a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases. In both cases the image lands sharply on the retina.

slides.heading: Near point and far point

rows: Closest distance at which an object is seen clearly without strain
About **25 cm** (least distance of distinct vision)
Farthest point up to which the eye sees clearly
Between the near point and the far point

visual.alt: Table: the near point is the closest distance seen clearly, about 25 centimetres for a normal young eye; the far point is the farthest, at infinity; the range of vision lies between them

slides.narration: Bring this screen slowly towards your nose. At some distance the words begin to blur and your eyes feel strained. That distance is your near point, about twenty-five centimetres for a healthy young adult. The far point is the farthest distance you can see clearly, which for a normal eye is infinity: you can see the Moon and the stars sharply.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much does the lens change?
slides.body_md: Treat the eye as one lens **2.0 cm** in front of the retina. Find its power when viewing (a) a very distant object, (b) an object at 25 cm.
bullets: Step 1 — the image is always on the retina, so $v = +2.0$ cm.
Step 2 — distant object: rays are parallel, so $f = 2.0$ cm $= 0.020$ m and $P = \dfrac{1}{0.020} = 50$ D.
Step 3 — object at 25 cm: $u = -25$ cm, so $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{2.0} - \dfrac{1}{-25} = 0.54$ per cm.
Step 4 — $f = \dfrac{1}{0.54} \approx 1.85$ cm, so $P = \dfrac{100}{1.85} \approx 54$ D.
Check — the power rises by about 4 D, which is exactly $\dfrac{1}{0.25\ \text{m}}$: the extra power needed to focus at 25 cm.

visual.alt: Table of results: distant object, focal length 2.0 centimetres and power 50 dioptres with relaxed ciliary muscles; object at 25 centimetres, focal length about 1.85 centimetres and power about 54 dioptres with contracted muscles

slides.narration: This uses the lens formula from the last chapter. The image distance never changes, because the retina does not move. For a far object the power is about fifty dioptres. To focus at twenty-five centimetres, the ciliary muscles squeeze the lens until its power is about fifty-four dioptres. That extra four dioptres is the accommodation a young eye can easily provide.

slides.heading: Quick check: a thicker lens
slides.body_md: When you look up from your book to a distant hill, what happens to your eye lens?
slides.narration: Think about which object is near and which is far. Then recall what the ciliary muscles do for a distant object, and what that does to the thickness and focal length of the lens.

slides.heading: Cataract: when the lens turns cloudy
slides.body_md: In some older people the eye lens becomes **milky and cloudy**. This condition, **cataract**, causes partial or complete loss of vision. It can be treated by **surgery** that replaces the cloudy lens.
slides.narration: Many grandparents have had a cataract operation. Their eye lens had slowly become milky, like frosted glass, so light could not pass through properly and everything looked hazy. In a short operation the cloudy lens is removed and replaced by an artificial one. Do not confuse cataract with the defects of focusing that we study next: in cataract the lens is not clear.

slides.heading: Three common defects of vision

visual.alt: Table of three defects: myopia, near objects clear and distant blurred, corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia, distant clear and near blurred, corrected by a convex lens; presbyopia with age, reading difficult, corrected by a convex or bifocal lens

slides.narration: The names can be confusing, so link each name to what the person can see. A near-sighted person sees near things well; that is myopia. A far-sighted person sees far things well; that is hypermetropia. Presbyopia comes with age and makes reading difficult. Learn the matching lens too: myopia needs concave, the other two need convex.

slides.heading: Myopia: image in front of the retina
slides.body_md: Causes: **excessive curvature** of the eye lens or **elongation of the eyeball**. The far point is closer than infinity.

slides.narration: In a myopic eye the light from a distant object is bent too much, or the eyeball is too long. Either way, the rays meet before they reach the retina and then spread out again, so the picture is blurred. The person sees clearly only up to a point called the far point. Panel c shows the cure: a concave lens of suitable power.

slides.heading: Choosing the lens for myopia
slides.body_md: The concave lens must make rays from a distant object **appear to come from the far point**. So its focal length equals the far-point distance, with a minus sign.

visual.alt: Table: far point 2 metres needs a lens of focal length minus 2 metres, power minus 0.5 dioptre; far point 50 centimetres needs minus 2 dioptres; far point 25 centimetres needs minus 4 dioptres

slides.narration: Here is the rule opticians use. A distant object sends parallel rays. The concave lens spreads them so they seem to start from the far point, where the myopic eye can focus. So the focal length of the lens is simply the far-point distance, negative because the lens is diverging. The closer the far point, the stronger the lens.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spectacles for a myopic student
slides.body_md: Anjali cannot read the blackboard clearly. Her far point is **1.5 m**. Find the nature and power of the lens she needs.
bullets: Step 1 — distant objects must appear to be at her far point: $v = -1.5$ m for $u = -\infty$.
Step 2 — so $f = -1.5$ m (diverging).
Step 3 — $P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-1.5} \approx -0.67$ D.

slides.narration: A hypermetropic person reads a signboard across the road easily but has to hold a book at arm’s length. The eye does not bend light enough, so rays from a near object would meet behind the retina. A convex lens adds the missing converging power. It makes rays from a book at twenty-five centimetres seem to come from the eye’s own, farther, near point.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading glasses
slides.body_md: Mr Rao’s near point is **50 cm**. What lens lets him read a newspaper held at 25 cm?
bullets: Step 1 — object at 25 cm: $u = -25$ cm. Its image must be at his near point: $v = -50$ cm (virtual, same side).
Step 2 — $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{50}$ per cm.
Step 4 — $P = \dfrac{1}{0.50} = +2$ D: a **convex lens** of power **+2 D**.
Check — positive power, converging lens, as hypermetropia needs.

visual.alt: Table of the solution: object distance minus 25 centimetres, image distance minus 50 centimetres, focal length plus 50 centimetres, power plus 2 dioptres

slides.narration: The trick is to see what the lens must do. The newspaper is at twenty-five centimetres, but Mr Rao can only focus at fifty. So the lens must form a virtual image of the paper at fifty centimetres. Put both distances, with negative signs, into the lens formula. The answer, plus two dioptres, is a convex lens.

slides.heading: Quick check: which lens?
slides.body_md: A student sees the blackboard clearly but finds her notebook blurred. Which lens corrects her vision?
slides.narration: Decide first what she can and cannot see clearly. Then name the defect. Only then match the defect to the lens.

slides.heading: Presbyopia and bifocal lenses
slides.body_md: With age the **ciliary muscles weaken** and the **eye lens loses flexibility**, so the near point moves away. Someone with both myopia and hypermetropia may need **bifocal lenses**: the **upper part concave** for distant vision, the **lower part convex** for reading.

visual.alt: Line graph of the typical near point against age: about 18 centimetres at age 10 and about 25 centimetres for young adults, rising slowly to about 26 centimetres at 40, then steeply to about 45 centimetres at 50 and about 90 to 110 centimetres after 60.
visual.caption: Illustrative values; they vary from person to person. Once the near point moves well beyond 25 cm, reading glasses are usually needed.

slides.narration: Look at the graph. The near point stays close to twenty-five centimetres until about forty, then climbs steeply. That is why many people in their forties start holding the newspaper further away. Spectacles with a convex lens help. Some people need help for both near and far vision; their bifocals have a concave upper part for looking ahead and a convex lower part for reading. Today contact lenses and surgery are also used.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cornea does most of the refraction; the lens fine-tunes focus; the retina forms a real, inverted image.
Iris controls pupil size; the pupil regulates the light entering.
Accommodation: ciliary muscles change the lens curvature; near point about 25 cm, far point infinity.
Myopia → concave lens, $f = -$(far point). Hypermetropia and presbyopia → convex lens.

rows: Lens too curved or eyeball too long
Focal length too long or eyeball too short

visual.alt: Summary table of the three defects with where the image forms, the cause and the corrective lens

slides.narration: Let us gather the key ideas. Know the job of each part of the eye, and how the ciliary muscles change the lens. Know the near and far points of a normal eye. For each defect, know where the image forms, the cause, and the lens that corrects it, including the sign of its power.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Do not write "the lens does most of the refraction": it is the **cornea**.
Myopia ↔ concave, hypermetropia ↔ convex. Write both the **name** and the **nature** (diverging/converging).
Ray diagrams: show the image in front of / behind the retina **and** the corrected eye with the lens drawn in front.
Powers: convert to metres; give the **sign** and unit D. Typical marks: formula (1) + substitution with signs (1) + answer with sign and unit (1).
Accommodation: muscles **relax** → lens **thin** → focal length **longer** (distant object).
slides.narration: Examiners see the same slips every year. Students swap the two lenses, forget the minus sign on a concave lens, or leave the power in per centimetre. In ray diagrams, draw the defective eye and the corrected eye, and mark where the image forms. And remember that relaxed ciliary muscles go with distant objects, not near ones.

slides.heading: The Colourful World
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a **glass prism** bends and splits light, how **raindrops** make a rainbow, and how the **atmosphere** bends and scatters sunlight.
slides.narration: After a monsoon shower the Sun comes out and a rainbow appears. At night the stars twinkle, but the planets shine steadily. And on a clear day the sky is a deep blue. All of these come from just two things light can do: bend when it changes medium, and bounce off tiny particles. Let us explore them one by one.

slides.heading: The triangular glass prism
slides.body_md: A prism has two triangular **bases** and three rectangular **lateral faces**. Light enters through one lateral face and leaves through another.

rows: The two lateral faces through which light enters and leaves
The angle between the two refracting faces
The face opposite the angle of the prism
Angle between the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray produced backward

visual.alt: Table of prism terms: refracting faces, angle of the prism between the two refracting faces, the base opposite it, and the angle of deviation between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray produced back

slides.narration: Hold a glass prism and look at its shape. Light usually enters one sloping face and leaves through the other. The angle between those two faces is called the angle of the prism. The face opposite this angle is the base. Keep these words handy: every prism question uses them.

slides.heading: Path of a ray through a prism
slides.body_md: At the first face light bends **towards the normal** (air to glass); at the second face it bends **away from the normal** (glass to air). The ray is bent **towards the base**.

At the second face it leaves into air and bends away from that face’s normal. Because the two faces are not parallel, the two bends add up instead of cancelling. rows: Parallel to the incident ray (only shifted sideways)

visual.alt: Comparison table: in a glass slab the faces are parallel and the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray with only a sideways shift; in a prism the faces are inclined, the emergent ray is turned towards the base and there is an angle of deviation

slides.narration: You traced rays through a glass slab in the last chapter. There the two faces are parallel, so the second bend exactly undoes the first, and the ray only shifts sideways. In a prism the faces meet at an angle, so the ray is turned. That single difference is why prisms can separate colours and slabs cannot.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: adding up the deviation
slides.body_md: For the ray on the diagram, $i = 48^\circ$, $r_1 = 29.7^\circ$, $r_2 = 30.3^\circ$ and $e = 49.2^\circ$. Find the angle of deviation.
bullets: Step 1 — at the first face the ray turns by $i - r_1 = 48^\circ - 29.7^\circ = 18.3^\circ$.
Step 2 — at the second face it turns by $e - r_2 = 49.2^\circ - 30.3^\circ = 18.9^\circ$.
Step 3 — both turns are towards the base, so they add: $\delta = 18.3^\circ + 18.9^\circ = 37.2^\circ$.
Check — $r_1 + r_2 = 60^\circ$, the angle of the prism, and $i + e - A = 48^\circ + 49.2^\circ - 60^\circ = 37.2^\circ$ too.

visual.alt: Table: the ray turns 18.3 degrees at the first face and 18.9 degrees at the second, both towards the base, a total deviation of 37.2 degrees

slides.narration: Deviation is just the total amount the ray has turned. At each face, the turn is the difference between the angle outside the glass and the angle inside. Both turns point towards the base, so we add them. Notice the neat check: the two angles inside the glass add up to the angle of the prism.

slides.heading: Why the colours separate
slides.body_md: Each colour bends through a **different angle**. **Red bends the least, violet the most**, so the colours fan out.

visual.alt: Table: red bends least and appears at the top of the spectrum when the prism apex points up; green is in between; violet bends most and appears at the bottom, nearest the base

slides.narration: Glass slows each colour by a slightly different amount, so each colour bends through a slightly different angle. Violet is bent the most and red the least. With the prism’s point upwards, everything is bent downwards towards the base, so violet ends up lowest and red highest on the screen.

slides.body_md: A second, identical prism placed **upside down** bends the colours back, and **white light** emerges. This shows that white light is a mixture of colours.

The first prism spread the colours apart; the inverted prism bent each colour back by exactly the same amount. Out came a beam of white light, parallel to the original. So the colours were in sunlight all along. Any light that gives a spectrum like sunlight is called white light.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: where should Kiran look?
slides.body_md: It is 4:30 in the evening in Kochi. A shower has just passed and the Sun is low in the **west**. Where should Kiran look for a rainbow?
bullets: Step 1 — a rainbow forms on the side **opposite the Sun**, so Kiran should turn his back to the Sun.
Step 2 — the Sun is in the west, so he should face **east**.
Step 3 — he needs raindrops in that direction: the departing rain clouds or mist in the east.
Step 4 — with the Sun low, the bow stands high above the horizon. At noon the Sun is high and the bow would be below the horizon, so rainbows are usually seen in the **morning or late afternoon**.

visual.alt: Table: in the morning, with the Sun in the east, look west; in the late afternoon, with the Sun in the west, look east; at noon the Sun is high and the rainbow is usually not visible

slides.narration: Rainbow-hunting is a neat use of the idea. The light comes from behind you and is sent back by the drops, so always stand with the Sun at your back. In the evening the Sun is in the west, so look east. Also, a low Sun gives a tall bow, which is why rainbows are a morning and evening treat.

slides.heading: Atmospheric refraction
slides.body_md: The **refractive index of air** changes with its temperature and density. Light passing through air layers of different refractive index **bends**; this is **atmospheric refraction**.

rows: Hot air (above a fire or a hot road)
Objects seen through it seem to waver

visual.alt: Table: hot air is less dense and optically rarer; cooler air is denser and optically denser; a moving mixture of the two makes objects seen through it appear to waver

slides.narration: Look at a distant object across a bonfire or a hot road in May and it seems to shimmer. The hot air just above is lighter and optically rarer than the cooler air around it, and the layers keep moving. Light passing through bends by changing amounts, so the apparent position of the object keeps wavering. The same thing happens, on a giant scale, in the whole atmosphere.

slides.heading: Stars twinkle, planets do not

rows: An extended source: many points together
Light reaching the eye flickers: brighter, dimmer
Flickers from different points average out

visual.alt: Comparison table: a star is extremely far and acts as a point source, so changing refraction makes its light flicker and it twinkles; a planet is closer and acts as an extended source made of many points whose flickers average out, so it shines steadily

slides.narration: Because the atmosphere is always changing, the path of starlight wobbles. A star is so far away that it is practically a single point, so the amount of its light entering your eye keeps changing: it twinkles. A planet is much closer and looks like a tiny disc. Each point on that disc flickers, but the flickers cancel out on average, so the planet glows steadily.

slides.narration: Sunlight contains all colours. As it passes through the air, the tiny molecules scatter blue light far more than red, because blue has a shorter wavelength. Red light has a wavelength about one point eight times that of blue. The scattered blue light reaches us from every direction in the sky, so the sky looks blue. Without an atmosphere there would be no scattering and the sky would look dark.

slides.narration: The colour of scattered light depends on the size of the particles. Very fine particles scatter mostly blue. Bigger particles scatter longer wavelengths as well, and if they are big enough, such as the water droplets in clouds, all colours are scattered alike and the light looks white. Passengers in aircraft flying very high see a darker sky, because there is little air above them to scatter light.

bullets: Prism: bends light towards the normal, then away; the ray turns towards the base by the angle of deviation.
Dispersion: white light → VIBGYOR; violet bends most, red least; an inverted prism recombines them.
Rainbow: refraction + dispersion, internal reflection, refraction in raindrops; Sun behind the observer.
Atmospheric refraction: twinkling stars, steady planets, Sun seen about 2 minutes early and late.
Scattering: Tyndall effect in colloids; tiny molecules scatter blue most → blue sky.

slides.narration: Four ideas run through this part. Deviation and dispersion happen in a prism. Raindrops combine dispersion with internal reflection to give a rainbow. Moving air of changing refractive index makes stars twinkle and gives us a few extra minutes of daylight. And scattering by particles explains the Tyndall effect and the blue sky.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In prism diagrams draw **normals** at both faces and mark $i$, $e$ and $\delta$; the emergent ray bends **towards the base**.
Write "violet deviates the most, red the least", not the other way round.
Rainbow answers need all three steps: **refraction with dispersion, internal reflection, refraction** — and "Sun behind the observer".
Twinkling: mention **point source**, **changing refractive index** and **flickering amount of light**. Planets: **extended source**, effects **average out**.
Blue sky: the particles are **smaller than the wavelength**, and **shorter wavelengths** are scattered more. Typical split: reason (1) + explanation (1) + example (1).
slides.narration: Most marks are lost by leaving out steps. A rainbow answer that mentions only refraction gets one mark, not three. A twinkling answer must say that the star is a point source. For the blue sky, link the size of the molecules to the wavelength of blue light. And in every prism diagram, draw the normals before you draw the rays.

sections.heading: 1. The human eye and accommodation
sections.body_md:
The eye is a nearly spherical organ about **2.3 cm** across that works like a camera.

- **Cornea**: transparent front bulge; **most refraction** happens at its outer surface.
- **Iris**: dark muscular diaphragm that **controls the size of the pupil**.
- **Pupil**: opening that **regulates the light** entering — small in bright light, large in dim light (the change takes time, which is why a dark hall looks black at first).
- **Eye lens**: crystalline, flexible; gives **fine adjustment** of focal length and forms a **real, inverted image** on the retina.
- **Ciliary muscles**: change the curvature of the lens.
- **Retina**: light-sensitive cells produce **electrical signals** that the **optic nerve** carries to the **brain**, which interprets them.

**Power of accommodation**: the ability of the lens to change its focal length. Distant object → ciliary muscles **relax** → lens **thin** → focal length **longer**. Near object → muscles **contract** → lens **thick** → focal length **shorter**. The focal length cannot be reduced below a minimum, so very near objects look blurred.

**Near point** (least distance of distinct vision): about **25 cm** for a normal young eye. **Far point**: **infinity**.

**Cataract**: the lens becomes milky and cloudy in some older people, causing partial or total loss of vision; treated by surgery.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length so that near and distant objects are both seen clearly.
The closest point at which an object can be seen clearly without strain; about 25 cm for a normal young eye.
The farthest point up to which the eye can see clearly; infinity for a normal eye.
Cloudiness of the eye lens that reduces vision; treated by surgery.

sections.heading: 2. Defects of vision and their correction
sections.body_md:
**Myopia (near-sightedness)**: near objects clear, distant objects blurred; the far point is nearer than infinity. The image of a distant object forms **in front of the retina**. Causes: **excessive curvature** of the eye lens; **elongation of the eyeball**. Correction: **concave lens** with $f = -$(far point distance).

**Hypermetropia (far-sightedness)**: distant objects clear, near objects blurred; the near point is farther than 25 cm. Light from a near object would focus **behind the retina**. Causes: **focal length of the lens too long**; **eyeball too small**. Correction: **convex lens** that forms a virtual image of an object at 25 cm at the person’s near point.

**Presbyopia**: with age the near point recedes because the **ciliary muscles weaken** and the **lens loses flexibility**. Correction: convex lens. A person with **both** myopia and hypermetropia uses **bifocal** lenses: **upper part concave** (distance), **lower part convex** (reading). Contact lenses and surgery are also used.

**Method for powers**: (1) decide the defect; (2) find $u$ and $v$ with signs (distances in front of the lens are negative); (3) use the lens formula; (4) convert $f$ to metres and find $P = 1/f$ with its sign.

key_terms.definition_md: Defect in which distant objects are blurred; corrected by a concave lens.
Defect in which near objects are blurred; corrected by a convex lens.
Age-related loss of accommodation; the near point moves away.
A lens with a concave upper part for distant vision and a convex lower part for near vision.

sections.heading: 3. Refraction through a glass prism
sections.body_md:
A **prism** has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral faces; the angle between the two **refracting faces** is the **angle of the prism** $A$.

At the **first face** light (air → glass) bends **towards the normal**; at the **second face** (glass → air) it bends **away from the normal**. Because the faces are inclined, the two bends add up and the emergent ray is turned **towards the base**.

The **angle of deviation** $\delta$ is the angle between the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray produced backward. Unlike a glass slab, the emergent ray is **not parallel** to the incident ray and $e \neq i$ in general.

**Drawing tip**: draw normals at both faces first; mark $i$, $r$, $e$ and $\delta$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle between the two refracting faces of a prism.
The angle between the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray produced backward.
The angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the second face.

sections.heading: 4. Dispersion of white light and the rainbow
sections.body_md:
**Dispersion**: splitting of white light into its component colours. The band of colours is a **spectrum**: **VIBGYOR**. Different colours bend through different angles: **violet the most, red the least**.

**Newton’s experiments**: (i) a second, identical prism placed **inverted** recombines the colours into **white light**, showing that white light is a mixture; (ii) a single colour from the spectrum passed through another prism is not split further. Any light that gives a spectrum like sunlight is called **white light**.

**Rainbow**: a natural spectrum seen after a shower. Water droplets act like small prisms: sunlight is **refracted and dispersed** on entering, **internally reflected**, and **refracted again** on leaving. A rainbow is always seen **opposite the Sun** — the Sun must be **behind** the observer. Red is on the **outer** edge, violet on the inner. It can also be seen in the spray of a waterfall or fountain.

sections.heading: 5. Atmospheric refraction
sections.body_md:
The refractive index of air depends on its **temperature and density**: hot air is lighter and **optically rarer**; cooler air is **optically denser**. Light passing through air of changing refractive index bends: **atmospheric refraction**.

- **Wavering objects** seen through hot air above a fire or a road: the moving hot and cool layers keep changing the refraction.
- **Apparent star position**: starlight bends towards the normal as it enters denser lower air, so a star appears **slightly higher** than it is (most noticeable near the horizon).
- **Twinkling of stars**: the atmosphere keeps changing, so the apparent position and the **amount of starlight entering the eye fluctuate**. Stars are so far away that they are **point sources**.
- **Planets do not twinkle**: they are much closer and act as **extended sources** (many point sources); the fluctuations **average out**.
- **Advance sunrise and delayed sunset**: the Sun is seen about **2 minutes before** it actually rises and about **2 minutes after** it actually sets, lengthening the apparent day by about 4 minutes.

key_terms.definition_md: Refraction of light by the Earth’s atmosphere, whose refractive index varies with temperature and density.
A source so distant that it appears as a single point, such as a star.

sections.heading: 6. Scattering of light
sections.body_md:
**Scattering**: redirection of light in many directions by particles in its path.

**Tyndall effect**: scattering by **colloidal particles** makes the path of a beam visible — a sunbeam in a smoky or dusty room, sunlight through the canopy of a misty forest, a torch beam in milk-water (but not in salt solution).

**Colour depends on particle size**: very fine particles scatter mainly **blue** (short wavelengths); larger particles scatter longer wavelengths too; particles large enough (cloud droplets) scatter all colours and look **white**.

**Blue sky**: air molecules and fine particles are **smaller than the wavelength** of visible light and scatter **blue much more than red** (red light has a wavelength about **1.8 times** that of blue). Scattered blue light reaches the eye from all over the sky. Without an atmosphere the sky would look **dark**; it does look much darker to passengers at very high altitudes, where scattering is not prominent.

key_terms.definition_md: Redirection of light in many directions by small particles.
Scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes the path of a beam visible.
